sections.h: Chapters 1-4: divisions, the cross and human wisdom
sections.b: Paul answers news from Chloe's people that the church was quarreling over its teachers. He rejects eloquence and status as the ground of faith, calls the cross the power and wisdom of God, and reminds the Corinthians that Paul, Apollos and Cephas are servants who all belong to them, as they belong to Christ.

common: Most scholars read chapters 1-4 as one argument about the Corinthians' pride in their teachers and in wisdom.
uncommon: F. C. Baur's view that the slogans in 1:12 name organized parties (a Petrine and a Pauline group) is now held by few.

sections.b: The letter shows a church in a Roman colony where status, patronage and public speaking counted for much. Most members were of ordinary rank, with a few leading households (Crispus, Gaius, Stephanas); Chloe's household sent word to Paul. Paul reminds them that "not many" were wise, powerful or well-born.
sections.refs: 1 Corinthians 1:2; 1 Corinthians 1:11; 1 Corinthians 1:14-16; 1 Corinthians 1:26-28; Acts 18:1-18; Romans 16:23

sections.h: Human wisdom and God's wisdom (1 Corinthians 1-4)
sections.b: Paul sets the wisdom of the world, which seeks signs and philosophy, against the foolishness of the cross, which is the wisdom of God. He quotes Isaiah 29:14, Job 5:13 and Psalm 94:11 to show that God overturns human cleverness, and he names Christ himself as "wisdom from God" (1:30). He draws on the Jewish picture of Wisdom as God's agent (Proverbs 8) without personifying her himself.

common: The cross is the center of Paul's answer to Corinthian pride.
uncommon: Some scholars read the "wisdom among the mature" (2:6) as Paul answering what the Corinthians themselves called wisdom.

sections.b: Paul calls himself an apostle by God's will, a planter, a master builder, a steward, a fool for Christ and a father. He came to Corinth in weakness, fear and trembling, supported himself by manual work, and would not build on rhetoric.

Apollos, an educated Jew of Alexandria (Acts 18:24), followed Paul in Corinth. Some Corinthians made him a rival leader (1:12; 3:4), but Paul says "Apollos watered", counts him a fellow worker, and later urged him to return (16:12).
sections.refs: 1 Corinthians 1:12; 1 Corinthians 3:4-9; 1 Corinthians 3:22; 1 Corinthians 4:6; 1 Corinthians 16:12; Acts 18:24-28; Acts 19:1

sections.b: Paul describes the apostles as the last in a procession, condemned men, a spectacle for angels and people, hungry, beaten and homeless, working with their hands. He places this against the Corinthians' boast that they already reign, and offers it as the shape of apostolic life.

sections.h: "Christ did not send me to baptize" (1 Corinthians 1:13-17)
sections.b: Paul is glad he baptized few in Corinth, because baptism "into the name of Paul" would make a party. He names Crispus, Gaius and the household of Stephanas, and says Christ sent him to tell the good news. Churches that baptize infants and churches that baptize only believers both cite the household of Stephanas (1:16).

sections.h: The Spirit and the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 2)
sections.b: Paul says his preaching came with "the proof of the Spirit and of power" (2:4), that the Spirit explores the depths of God and reveals them (2:10-12), that the person without the Spirit does not accept these things (2:14), and that the church is the temple where the Spirit lives (3:16).

sections.h: The church as God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16-17)
sections.b: Paul tells the Corinthians together that they are God's temple (naos, the inner house where God's presence lived), where his Spirit lives, and warns that anyone who ruins this temple, by splitting the church over human wisdom, will be ruined by God. The Qumran community also described itself as a temple of people.

sections.h: The word of the cross (1 Corinthians 1-2)
sections.b: Paul preaches "Christ crucified", a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles, and decides to know nothing among the Corinthians but Jesus Christ and him crucified. In Rome crucifixion was the punishment of slaves and rebels; in the Torah a hanged man is under God's curse (Deuteronomy 21:23).

Paul calls the Corinthians "the church of God" and asks them to be knit together in one mind. He uses the images of a field, a building and God's temple. Churches differ on what the unity he asks for requires (see the card at 1:10).

sections.h: The Day that tests the builders (1 Corinthians 3:10-15; 4:3-5)
sections.b: Each builder's work will be tested by fire on the Day. The work that stays earns a reward; the work that burns is lost, though the builder is saved. Paul asks the Corinthians not to judge before the Lord comes, who will bring hidden things to light and give each person praise from God.

Paul says a builder whose work is burned up "will be saved, but only as if through fire". The Catholic Church cites the verse in its teaching on purgatory (with the Councils of Florence and Trent), while Lutheran, Reformed and Anglican churches read the fire as the judgment itself or as the testing of works. Orthodox churches do not take over the Latin teaching, and Orthodox writers differ on the fire.

"Cephas" is Peter's Aramaic name. Some Corinthians said "I belong to Cephas" (1:12). Paul puts Cephas beside himself and Apollos as belonging to the church (3:22) and names Christ as the only foundation (3:11).

sections.h: The kingdom of God in power (1 Corinthians 4:20)
sections.b: Paul says the kingdom of God is not talk but power. Some in Corinth already claimed to reign (4:8); Paul replies that the kingdom is present in the weakness of the apostles until Christ returns.

sections.h: The day of our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 1:8)
sections.b: Paul takes the prophets' phrase and speaks of "the day of our Lord Jesus Christ" when the Corinthians will be free of blame. In chapters 3 and 4 the Day is when works are tested and hidden motives shown.
Paul speaks God's wisdom "in a mystery", hidden before the ages and now revealed through the Spirit, and calls himself and Apollos stewards of God's mysteries.

sections.h: The rulers of this age (1 Corinthians 2:6-8)
sections.b: Paul says the rulers of this age did not understand God's wisdom or they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. Interpreters read these as human rulers, as spiritual powers, or as both.
This five-word saying has no verb. It has been read as a rule to stay within Scripture, as a reference to the passages Paul has just quoted, as a school maxim or as a later note.
Paul says God chose the foolish, weak and low things of the world to shame the wise and strong. The choice is of a kind of people, those of low rank, in the context of a church proud of its rank.
Christ became for us wisdom from God, righteousness, holiness and redemption. In 4:4 Paul uses "justified" for the last verdict: a clear conscience does not decide it.

sections.h: "What do you have that you did not receive?" (1 Corinthians 4:7)
sections.b: Augustine cited this verse against Pelagius to show that all good is a gift of grace; churches that follow him and those that stress human response use it differently.
Hungry, thirsty, poorly clothed, beaten and homeless, the apostles bless those who insult them. Paul uses the traditional list of hardships to show weakness as the mark of the gospel.
The main questions in these chapters are: "you were baptized" or "I baptized" (1:15), "testimony" or "mystery" (2:1), "dissensions" (3:3) and the verbless phrase of 4:6.
Paul sets Greek love of wisdom beside Jewish demand for signs. In Corinth a culture of public speaking and philosophy made eloquence a mark of status.
